title: The anthropogenic fingerprint on emerging infectious diseases.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Listed the Zenodo record (one 600,874,624-byte zip, CC-BY-4.0) and the full GitHub tree. Downloaded and parsed 11 per-disease model tables (output/model_df/*_df_wp.csv), the 50,000-row global background file, the covariate dictionary and the processed dengue outbreak file. Counted presences per disease (dengue 11,313; CCHF 1,481; Chagas 1,219; melioidosis 521; chikungunya 458; Lassa 415; RVF 353; H5N1 193; P. knowlesi 122; MERS 63; Ebola 30; total 16,168), background rows, duplicate coordinates and missingness. Read the per-disease modelling script header (background points weighted by population, 2-8x presences).
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The 58,319 records, 32 diseases, 16 drivers, 169 countries, 1910-2022 and the 32% per-hour reporting decline come from the abstract and press coverage; no full text was available (paywalled, no PMCID). I did not check the paper's per-disease counts against the files, and I did not open the 600 MB Zenodo zip (over the size cap).

a1_downloadable.note: Public GitHub raw files downloaded without login; Zenodo archive is CC-BY-4.0. Only 11-13 of the 32 diseases are shared: the README says the rest came from non-public sources.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Checked in files: a 'presence' column (1 = outbreak record, 0 = background point) is in every model table. The zeros are sampled background points, not observed absences.

a3_inputs_present.note: Checked in files: 21 numeric driver covariates (forest cover, livestock density, travel time to a health facility, temperature change, etc.) are already extracted per row, plus longitude/latitude.

a4_units_stated.note: covariate_lookup.csv describes each covariate (e.g. 'Proportion cropland cover 2015'); some units, such as minutes of travel time, are implied by the source products rather than stated in a column.

a5_enough_rows.note: Counted: 41,224 rows across the 11 public disease tables (16,168 presences), plus 50,000 global background rows. Dengue alone has 23,421 rows. Ebola (30) and MERS (63) presences are tiny.

a6_fits_laptop.note: All model tables together are under 40 MB; nothing needs a GPU.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: The public subset (16,168 presences) is far below the paper's 58,319 records, but the README explains why (non-public sources withheld). Dengue's processed file has 12,668 rows and its model table 11,313 presences, so some filtering happened between them. I could not check per-disease counts without the full text.

a8_label_provenance.note: Presences are reported outbreak events from literature compilations (IHME), ministries of health and surveillance, so they are real observations, not model output. The zeros are population-weighted random background points, so 'presence vs background' partly measures where people live and report, not true absence.

B1.why: 11 per-disease CSVs plus a global background CSV, all sharing one 28-column schema; pooling is a concat.

B2.why: Every CSV parsed first try with pandas; numeric covariates are clean.

B3.why: Presences mix point and admin-polygon records from IHME, ministries and surveillance; covariates harmonised by authors.

B4.why: No censored values seen; but 'hunting' covariate is 50-79% missing in several tables.

B5.why: 4,656 of 11,313 dengue presences share coordinates with another; easy to dedupe or group.

B6.why: covariate_lookup.csv documents 21 covariates; record_id and ADMcode codes are undocumented.

C1.why: Leave-one-disease-out transfer is informative either way: it tests the paper's claim that drivers are disease-specific.

C2.why: Per-disease niche maps (e.g. Ebola, eLife 2014) and authors' INLA models exist; no cross-disease predictive transfer found.

C3.why: Unique application: predictive transfer across 11 harmonised diseases and location-embedding features, versus the paper's inferential models.

C4.why: Outbreak surveillance is costly, but risk mapping itself is a cheap desk exercise already done per disease.

C5.why: Obvious dummies: travel-time-only and population-only classifiers; logistic regression on the 16 drivers.

D1.why: SatCLIP, a location encoder from satellite imagery, has open weights (GitHub licence checked: MIT).

D2.why: Embeddings come from latitude/longitude alone; about 90k points embed once on CPU.

D3.why: SatCLIP is MIT; data archive CC-BY-4.0, though underlying IHME sources carry their own terms.

E1.why: Spatial block, leave-one-disease-out and leave-one-region-out splits are all buildable from coordinates and files seen.

E2.why: 11 public diseases; dengue alone large enough for many spatial blocks.

E3.why: Population-weighted background rate and a travel-time-only model are easy dummies.

E4.why: No replicate measurements; duplicate coordinates are repeat events, not repeat measurements.

E5.why: Paper reports reporting falls with travel time to health facility; model must recover that negative effect.

E6.why: Label shuffling and covariate-block ablation are straightforward on the flat tables.

E7.why: Held-out diseases or regions; processed outbreak files carry a Year column (dengue 1985-2015) for a temporal split.

E8.why: example_pipeline reproduces dengue, Chagas and H5N1 INLA coefficients; published params CSVs available to compare.

G1.why: Every row has longitude/latitude; presences also carry GAUL/GADM admin codes.

G2.why: SatCLIP embeddings or WorldPop/ERA5 rasters join on coordinates directly.

G3.why: Points join one-to-one; polygon-level presences need an aggregation rule.

G4.why: Embeddings could show what the 16 hand-picked drivers miss, but that is a modest extension.

H1.why: Negatives are only population-weighted pseudo-absences; true absence of outbreaks is never recorded.

H2.why: 11 diseases over several continents, but each disease is usually one source (IHME for dengue).

H3.why: Claim is precisely statable: separates reported outbreak sites from population-weighted background.

H4.why: Paper models reporting bias explicitly; README states non-public diseases are withheld.

I1.why: Verena / viralemergence consortium (Gibb, Carlson) and One Health surveillance planners.

I2.why: A transfer result could shape whether multi-disease risk maps are used; marginal for single-disease planners.

I3.why: AUC on presence-background roughly matches 'where to surveil', but not a calibrated outbreak probability.

I4.why: Nonlinear covariate effects help, but travel time alone may explain much; must test first.

J1.why: Real modelling: spatial CV, transfer across tasks, frozen embeddings plus head.

J2.why: Disease ecology intuition needed to judge maps; paper's coefficients give a reference.

J3.why: Even a spatial-CV benchmark of the 11 public tables is a shareable result.

J4.why: Scope feasible in about two weeks but not yet written down.

J5.why: Kill condition stated below; date not yet in NOTES.md.

existing_models.name: Gibb et al. 2026 INLA geospatial logistic regression (this paper)
existing_models.score_and_split: Inferential Bayesian models with a spatial random effect, compared by information criteria; no held-out predictive score seen in the files I opened.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Abstract: directly transmitted zoonoses (Ebola, mpox) share few common drivers, and observed geography is dominated by healthcare access.

existing_models.name: Pigott et al. 2014, Ebola zoonotic niche map (eLife), boosted regression trees
existing_models.score_and_split: Not retrieved in detail; seen only as a search result.

existing_models.name: Integrated machine-learning framework for zoonotic spillover across modified landscapes (Environmental Health Perspectives, 2026), CatBoost gradient boosting
existing_models.score_and_split: Mean R-squared 0.72 under 10-fold random cross-validation (from the search snippet), so spatial leakage is likely.

backbone.name: SatCLIP (satellite-imagery location encoder, Microsoft)
backbone.hardware: Laptop CPU; embed about 90k coordinates once, then gradient boosting or logistic head

integration.partner_dataset: SatCLIP location embeddings (or WorldPop population and ERA5 climate rasters)
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Do general-purpose satellite-derived location features predict where outbreaks of a held-out disease get reported better than the 16 hypothesis-driven anthropogenic drivers?

controls.positive_control: Recover the paper's negative effect of travel time to a health facility on reporting, and dengue's known positive association with urban cover and temperature.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle presence labels within each disease and confirm AUC falls to 0.5; train on travel time plus population alone to measure how much is reporting bias.
controls.external_validation: Leave-one-disease-out and leave-one-region-out (dengue/yellow fever arboregions exist in outputs), plus a temporal split using the Year column in output/spillovers_processed.

honest_claim_h3: Among 11 publicly shareable diseases, the model separates places where outbreaks were reported from population-weighted random places, which mixes true outbreak risk with where surveillance reaches.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use land-use, climate and healthcare-access features at a location to predict whether an outbreak of a given disease was reported there.
plain_idea.train_on: One row per outbreak record or random background point, with 21 pre-extracted environmental and social features; 41,224 rows across 11 diseases (16,168 outbreak records), verified in files.
plain_idea.predict: Whether the row is a reported outbreak (1) or a population-weighted random background point (0); outbreaks come from literature compilations, ministries of health and surveillance reports.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Tests whether a model trained on some diseases can map risk for another, which decides whether multi-disease risk maps are worth building for poorly recorded diseases; a failure confirms the paper's 'no one-size-fits-all' claim with predictive evidence.

more_or_better_data.why: 11 diseases with one shared, harmonised covariate set (41,224 rows) is broader than single-disease maps like Ebola's, but it is only the public part of the paper's 58,319 records, and most sources (IHME) were already used by earlier maps.

confidence_score.why: No replicate measurements, and the background zeros are not true absences, so a calibrated outbreak probability is not supported; the paper's INLA models already give posterior uncertainty.

models_beatable.why: The paper's 2026 INLA models are inferential, not tuned for held-out prediction, and the 2026 CatBoost study used random 10-fold cross-validation; an honest spatial-block comparison has not been seen.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Adding SatCLIP embeddings gives the model more information, but they do not measure the same quantity, and spatial autocorrelation may make gains illusory; improvement is not guaranteed.

label_elsewhere.sources: IHME occurrence databases for dengue, MERS and RVF (bundled in the repo, seen); global compendia for CCHF and Chagas (bundled, seen); WHO Disease Outbreak News and ProMED exist (known resources, not checked).
label_elsewhere.why: Further outbreak reports could serve as an external test of held-out locations, but they are scattered, have mixed formats and largely overlap the sources already used.

risks: Repeated outbreaks at the same coordinates (4,656 of 11,313 dengue presences share a location) would land in both train and test under a random split.
Spatial autocorrelation: nearby points share covariates, so random cross-validation inflates the score.
Background points are population-weighted, so population-linked features (urban cover, travel time) can separate classes through sampling design rather than biology.
Polygon-level presences were assigned covariates by the authors' buffering, which differs from point rows and could correlate with source and region.
leakage_plan.split: Spatial block cross-validation (for example 500 km blocks built from the Longitude/Latitude columns, seen in files), plus leave-one-disease-out and leave-one-region-out; group identical coordinates in the same fold.
checks: Shuffle presence labels and confirm AUC drops to about 0.5.
Fit travel time plus population density alone and report how much of the full model's AUC it reaches.
Compare random-split and spatial-block AUC; a large gap shows spatial leakage.
Measure each test point's distance to the nearest training point.
leakage_plan.verdict: Manageable for spatial leakage, but the population-weighted background is a serious structural confound that no split removes.

success_criteria.metric: Spatial-block AUC (area under the ROC curve) on held-out diseases (leave-one-disease-out), because the use is ranking unsurveyed places for a disease with poor records.
success_criteria.baselines: AUC of a travel-time plus population-only model and of logistic regression on the 16 drivers, on the same spatial blocks (not yet computed; no published held-out number found).
success_criteria.success: Pooled cross-disease model beats the disease's own logistic-regression-on-drivers baseline by at least 0.05 AUC on at least 5 of 11 held-out diseases, or SatCLIP features add at least 0.05 AUC over the 16 drivers under spatial-block CV.
success_criteria.kill: If travel time plus population alone reaches within 0.03 AUC of the full model under spatial-block CV for dengue, stop: the signal is reporting bias.

ambitious.why: Publishes cross-disease One Health risk modelling; would need clear positive cross-disease transfer that survives the reporting-bias control.

realistic.why: Fits a methods-and-evaluation study of spatial transfer and location embeddings for outbreak mapping, including a mixed result.

fallback.journal: medRxiv preprint plus a Climate Change AI or Machine Learning for Global Health workshop paper
fallback.why: A negative result (signal is mostly reporting bias, no transfer) is still a useful benchmark note.

pitch.headline: One harmonised 21-feature table for 11 emerging diseases, 16,168 outbreak records, ready to model in pandas.
pitch.what_makes_the_data_unusual: Same covariates extracted the same way for dengue, CCHF, Chagas, Lassa, RVF, H5N1, MERS, Ebola and others, plus 50,000 global background points; CC-BY-4.0 archive.
pitch.the_win: A leave-one-disease-out spatial AUC showing whether a pooled model maps a held-out disease's reported outbreaks better than its own driver-based model.
pitch.even_if_it_fails: We learn how much of mapped outbreak 'risk' is just healthcare access and population sampling, quantified under honest spatial splits.
pitch.who_wants_it: The Verena / viralemergence consortium (Gibb, Carlson) and One Health surveillance planners deciding whether multi-disease risk maps can stand in for missing single-disease data.

ml_idea: Pool the 11 public per-disease presence/background tables; train gradient boosting on the 21 drivers, with and without frozen SatCLIP location embeddings; evaluate with spatial-block and leave-one-disease-out CV against a travel-time plus population reporting-bias baseline.

effort.compute_note: Estimated from file sizes (under 40 MB total) and row counts; SatCLIP on about 90k coordinates is a small CPU forward pass; nothing was timed.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: On dengue (23,421 rows), compare spatial-block AUC of travel time plus population against all 21 drivers; if the gap is under 0.03, the project is about reporting bias.

verdict_reason: Clean, harmonised public tables for 11 diseases pass Part A. But the zeros are population-weighted background points, and only 16,168 of the paper's 58,319 records are public, so first check that the drivers beat a travel-time plus population baseline under spatial-block CV.
